flashcards.q: What is structured logging?
flashcards.a: Writing each log line as fields, like JSON, so a machine can filter and count by them.
flashcards.more: Plain sentences are easy for people to read, but a machine can't pull an order_id or gateway out of them. In a JSON log every fact has its own field. So in a log tool, searching "order_id = 5512" brings up every line of that order.

flashcards.q: Why keep the log message fixed and put the changing facts in the context?
flashcards.a: A fixed message groups the same event under one name, which makes counting, graphs and alerts easy. Facts in separate fields can be filtered.
flashcards.more: To a machine, "Payment failed for order 5512" and "Payment failed for order 5513" are two different messages. If the message is always "payment.failed" and order_id sits in the context, "how many payment.failed in the last hour?" is a single query.

flashcards.q: What is a correlation ID?
flashcards.a: A tracking number for one request, identical across every service, queue, worker and log line it touches.
flashcards.more: Like a package's tracking number: wherever it's scanned, the same number is written down. Type the number into your log tool and the lines from the API, the payment service and the worker line up in time order. Now you can read the whole story of one request.

flashcards.q: Where is a correlation ID created, and what if the request already has one?
flashcards.a: At the first door into your system. If an upstream service already sent one in a header, validate it and reuse it instead of making a new one.
flashcards.more: If every service invents its own number, the chain breaks and one service's logs can't be matched with another's. But don't trust an outside value blindly: check its shape (a UUID, say), or someone can push junk into your logs.

flashcards.q: What does a Monolog processor do?
flashcards.a: It runs just before each log record is written and adds extra data to it, such as the correlation ID or user ID.
flashcards.more: In Symfony, put `#[AsMonologProcessor]` on a class and it becomes a processor. It receives the `LogRecord` and adds data to its `extra` part. The gain: you change nothing in the hundreds of places that write logs. One place adds the data to every line.

flashcards.q: How does a correlation ID get across a queue to the worker?
flashcards.a: It travels with the message as a stamp. On the worker side, a Messenger middleware reads the stamp and makes the number current.
flashcards.more: A worker is a separate process, often on another server, so it can't see a number held in the request's memory. At dispatch time the middleware stamps the number onto the message. On the other side the same middleware sees the `ReceivedStamp`, knows it's in a worker, and sets the number again.

flashcards.q: How can every outgoing HTTP call carry the correlation ID without anyone remembering?
flashcards.a: Decorate Symfony's HTTP client with a class whose request() method adds the X-Correlation-Id header, then forwards the call.
flashcards.more: Adding the header by hand works until someone forgets it once, and the trail is cut exactly there. A decorator does it in one place for every call made through the default client. Scoped clients are separate services and need the same decoration.

flashcards.q: One order is lost among 40,000 log lines. How do you find its story?
flashcards.a: Get its correlation ID (from the response header or the customer's screenshot) and filter every service's logs by it.
flashcards.more: Filtering by one number leaves only that request's lines from the API, the payment service and the worker, in time order. It only works for lines logged after the number was added, so set it up before an incident.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between a trace and a span?
flashcards.a: A trace is one request's whole journey. A span is one step of it, with a start time, a duration and a parent span.
flashcards.more: A checkout trace might hold five spans: the whole request, the cart query, the payment API call, the order insert and the queue message. Lay them side by side and the longest one is the cause of the slowness. The trace ID travels between services in the `traceparent` header.

flashcards.q: Which question do logs, metrics and traces each answer?
flashcards.a: Log: exactly what happened. Metric: how often and how fast. Trace: where one request's time went.
flashcards.more: The three don't replace one another. A metric tells you there is a problem ("errors went up"). A trace shows which step it is in. A log says exactly what happened in that step. If all three carry the same correlation or trace ID, you can jump from one to the next. More in [[observability/metrics-slos/average-lies|metrics and SLOs]].

flashcards.q: What must never be written to a log?
flashcards.a: Passwords, tokens, API keys, card numbers and any personal data you don't need.
flashcards.more: Logs reach many people and many tools, sit around for months, and are usually guarded less strictly than a database. A secret in a log is as good as a leaked secret. For identity, user_id or order_id is enough, with no need for an email or phone number.

flashcards.q: Why isn't average response time enough?
flashcards.a: An average hides a few very slow requests. p90 and p99 show the experience of your slowest customers.
flashcards.more: If 99 of 100 customers get 100ms and one gets 3 seconds, the average is about 130ms, which looks lovely. Yet that one customer may be the one with the biggest cart. So always measure latency with percentiles.

flashcards.q: What does p99 latency mean?
flashcards.a: The time within which 99 out of 100 customers got their answer. The remaining 1 waited longer.
flashcards.more: p50 is the middle customer's experience, p99 is close to the slowest customer's. In a large system one page load makes many requests, so p99 is often the normal experience for a given user.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between a counter, a gauge and a histogram?
flashcards.a: A counter only goes up, a gauge goes up and down, and a histogram counts values into buckets so you can get percentiles.
flashcards.more: Counter: total requests. Gauge: how many messages are in the queue right now. Histogram: how long requests took, split into buckets. You rarely read a counter's raw value; you use `rate()` to see "how many per second".

flashcards.q: What goes wrong if you put user_id in a metric label?
flashcards.a: A cardinality explosion: each user becomes a separate time series, so memory and cost blow up.
flashcards.more: Every distinct combination of label values is its own time series. A route (a few dozen) is fine; a user_id (millions) is not. Following one particular user is a job for logs or traces, not metrics.

flashcards.q: Why can't a PHP-FPM app keep Prometheus metrics in plain memory?
flashcards.a: Each request is a short-lived process, so in-memory counters start from zero every time. Store them in Redis or APCu.
flashcards.more: Redis gives one shared set of numbers for all servers, at the price of a network call per write. APCu is faster, but each server then holds only its own numbers. Prometheus scrapes every server either way.

flashcards.q: What are RED and USE?
flashcards.a: RED for services: Rate, Errors, Duration. USE for machines: Utilization, Saturation, Errors.
flashcards.more: RED measures the user's experience: how many requests, how many fail, how slow. USE measures the health of a resource: how busy the CPU is, how long the queue is, how often it failed. RED tells you what is broken, USE tells you why.

flashcards.q: What is saturation and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: More work is waiting in line than the machine can handle. It is an early warning of delays.
flashcards.more: The CPU can show 40% busy while 10,000 messages sit in the queue because there are too few workers. That piled-up work (saturation) later comes back as delay for users. So always measure queue depth and connection pool waits.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between SLI, SLO and SLA?
flashcards.a: SLI: a measured ratio. SLO: its target. SLA: a contract with the customer, with penalties if broken.
flashcards.more: An SLI is, say, "successful checkouts within 500ms / all checkouts". An SLO is, say, "99.9% over 30 days". An SLA is usually looser than the SLO, so you get a warning before you break your own target.

flashcards.q: What is the error budget for a 99.9% SLO over 30 days?
flashcards.a: About 43 minutes of failure, or 1,000 failed requests per million.
flashcards.more: The math: 30 days = 43,200 minutes. 0.1% = 43.2 minutes. At 99.99% it is only about 4 minutes. Each extra 9 costs many times more, so giving every service the same high SLO is wasteful.

flashcards.q: What does a burn rate of 14.4 mean for a 99.9% SLO?
flashcards.a: Failures are arriving 14.4 times faster than the SLO allows. At that speed the 30-day budget is gone in about 2 days.
flashcards.more: One hour at 14.4x burns 2% of the 30-day budget (14.4 / 720 hours). That is fast enough to page someone. A slower burn, say 6x over 6 hours, only needs a ticket. Two tiers keep pages for real emergencies.

flashcards.q: How does an error budget help you make decisions?
flashcards.a: While budget remains, ship features fast; when it runs low, pause features and work on stability. The rule is written in advance.
flashcards.more: Features vs stability turns into a fight of opinions. A budget gives both sides one shared number. With a rule agreed on beforehand, the decision during a crisis needs no argument.

flashcards.q: What is alert fatigue?
flashcards.a: When there are too many useless alerts, the team learns to ignore them, and the alert for a real crisis gets missed too.
flashcards.more: If a fire alarm goes off by mistake every day, nobody leaves the building anymore. Alerts work the same way: reduce or delete any alert that rings with nothing to do. The goal is that on every page, a person really does something.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between liveness and readiness probes?
flashcards.a: Liveness: "are you stuck, do you need a restart?" On failure, restart. Readiness: "can you take requests now?" On failure, stop traffic.
flashcards.more: When readiness fails the process doesn't die; the load balancer just leaves it out for a while and brings it back when it recovers. They need separate endpoints, because the questions differ and so does the consequence of failing.

flashcards.q: Why is checking the database in a liveness probe a mistake?
flashcards.a: When the database goes down, every server restarts at once, and a restart doesn't fix the database. The problem only grows.
flashcards.more: Liveness should speak only for itself: can PHP answer? The state of outside dependencies is readiness's job. Otherwise one dependency's trouble turns into a restart storm across the whole fleet.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between a shallow and a deep health check?
flashcards.a: Shallow only answers for itself. Deep also touches dependencies like the database or cache.
flashcards.more: Shallow is cheap and stable, so it suits liveness. Deep tells you more but is slower and more fragile, so readiness uses it only for essential dependencies. If a deep check includes a third-party API, their outage takes you down too.

flashcards.q: Which HTTP status does a failing readiness endpoint return?
flashcards.a: 503 (Service Unavailable). 200 when it succeeds.
flashcards.more: 503 says "not now, try later". Most load balancers, Kubernetes included, treat 2xx/3xx as success and anything else as failure. Don't put internal error details in the response body; they belong in the log.

flashcards.q: Should you page on symptoms or on causes?
flashcards.a: On symptoms: user harm (errors, slowness, SLO burn). For causes (CPU, disk), use a ticket or a dashboard.
flashcards.more: Customers may notice nothing at 90% CPU, and checkout may be broken at 30% CPU. A symptom-based alert handles both correctly. You hunt for the cause after the alert, on the dashboard.

flashcards.q: What are the three conditions of a good alert?
flashcards.a: Urgent (harm now), actionable (a person can do something), and it has a runbook.
flashcards.more: An alert with nothing to do belongs on a dashboard. An alert with something to do that isn't urgent belongs in a ticket. Page only when all three hold. Every page should also name an owning team.

flashcards.q: What is a runbook and what goes in it?
flashcards.a: A one-page guide for when an alert fires: what it means, what to look at first, likely causes, how to stop it, who to call.
flashcards.more: A sleepy brain at 2 a.m. can't think from scratch. A runbook puts past experience to work. Update it after every incident. If the alert rule's `runbook_url` annotation links to it, it's one click away.

flashcards.q: Why add a minimum-traffic condition to an error-ratio alert?
flashcards.a: With very little traffic one failed request is already a big percentage. A floor such as 12 requests a minute stops pages at 3 a.m. over a single error.
flashcards.more: Example: 4 checkouts in 5 minutes and 1 fails is 25%, above the 5% line, though nothing is really wrong. The rule says "ratio above 5% and more than 0.2 requests a second".

flashcards.q: Why put `for` in an alert rule?
flashcards.a: So the alert fires only when the condition holds continuously for that long, not on a momentary spike.
flashcards.more: A one-moment error spike is normal, caused by a deploy or retries. `for: 5m` means "5 minutes in a row". Too long and you hear late, too short and you get false alerts, so choose by looking at your SLO and the kind of harm.

flashcards.q: In an incident, what comes first: finding the cause or stopping the harm?
flashcards.a: Stopping the harm (mitigate). Finding the cause comes after the harm stops, calmly.
flashcards.more: With a burst pipe, shut the valve first and look for the cause afterwards. Rollback, turning a feature flag off, scaling up or failing over are the fast ways to stop harm. While the harm continues, every minute costs customers and money.

flashcards.q: What is triage?
flashcards.a: Measuring the harm (who, how badly, since when) and setting priorities, so attention goes to the most urgent work first.
flashcards.more: Like a hospital emergency room: the person hurt worst goes first. In the first five minutes, ask who is hurt, how badly, since when, what changed, and whether money or data is at risk. The answers set the severity.

flashcards.q: What are SEV1, SEV2 and SEV3?
flashcards.a: Levels of incident severity: SEV1 is the most serious (money or data at risk), SEV3 the most minor.
flashcards.more: For each level it is decided in advance how many people get involved, how fast they respond, and how often updates go out. When in doubt, rate it higher; you can lower it later. With definitions written down, nobody argues at 3 a.m.

flashcards.q: Why is "what changed?" the most useful question to ask early?
flashcards.a: Most outages follow a recent deploy, config or traffic change, so that is the likeliest guess.
flashcards.more: Find the outage's start time and match it against what was deployed just before. If they line up, rollback is the fastest and safest path. If not, check whether traffic or an outside dependency changed.

flashcards.q: Which mitigation is the safest, and which the riskiest?
flashcards.a: Safest: rollback, turning the feature flag off. Then scaling, and last a hotfix: new code, new risk.
flashcards.more: A rollback returns to a previously tested state. A hotfix is new code written under incident pressure, often without proper tests. So roll back first where you can, and be careful with migrations (a dropped column can't be restored).

flashcards.q: Why can't you always fix a bad deploy by rolling back?
flashcards.a: Rollback restores the code, not the database. If the deploy renamed or dropped a column, the old code breaks on the new schema.
flashcards.more: Change the schema in two deploys: expand (add the new column, keep the old one) and, days later, contract (drop the old one). The price is two deploys and a period with data in two columns. For a brand-new table nobody reads yet, one step is fine.

flashcards.q: What does an Incident Commander do, and not do?
flashcards.a: They coordinate, decide and divide the work. They don't debug or work on the keyboard themselves.
flashcards.more: The commander holds the whole picture: who is doing what, what has changed, who needs to be called. Pick up a task and your attention locks onto one thing and you lose the rest. The other roles are the Ops lead, Comms lead and Scribe.

flashcards.q: What goes in a good status update?
flashcards.a: The impact (in numbers), what we know, what we're doing, what we don't know, and the time of the next update.
flashcards.more: Writing "what we don't know" is a sign of honesty; passing a guess off as fact costs trust. Naming the next update's time means nobody keeps asking. Keeping stakeholders informed is one person's specific job.

flashcards.q: What is a blameless postmortem?
flashcards.a: After an incident, asking "why did the system let this happen?" instead of "who is to blame?", and writing an action list with owners and dates.
flashcards.more: People will make mistakes; the system has to be built so one mistake doesn't become a disaster. Hunt for blame and people hide mistakes, and learning stops. A postmortem holds a timeline, the impact, the root cause, what went well and badly, and an action list.

flashcards.q: What must every item in a postmortem's action list have?
flashcards.a: One owner and one date. An action with no owner usually never gets done.
flashcards.more: Put the actions in tickets and track them, and check at the next meeting how many are done. The best actions prevent a repeat: a new alert, a new test, a new guardrail. "We'll be more careful" is not an action.
